title: How I built a real-time editorial filter that catches AI slop in interactive fiction — 275 rules, zero latency, running on every response
author: Jaycool2k
selftext:
I've been building an interactive AI roleplay engine where the AI plays narrator, NPCs, and the entire world while the player controls their character. Think AI Dungeon but with a focus on prose quality — the kind of writing you'd actually want to read, not the "palpable tension hung in the air as she squared her shoulders" default that every LLM produces.

The core technical challenge: **how do you make generative AI produce fiction-quality prose in real-time, consistently, across thousands of exchanges?**

Here's the architecture I landed on after 6 months of iteration.

**The problem: LLMs have default vocabulary**

If you generate 100 pieces of fiction with any frontier model, you'll find the same constructions appearing at wildly non-human rates. "The air crackled with tension." "A kaleidoscope of emotions." "Despite herself." "The ghost of a smile." "Squared their shoulders." Em dashes at 3-5x the human rate. Semicolons everywhere. Three-item lists (tricolon) as a default rhythm.

These aren't bad phrases individually. But they're statistical defaults — the path of least resistance in the model's probability distribution. Human writers use them occasionally. AI uses them *systematically*. Readers can't always articulate why AI writing feels off, but this is a big part of it.

**Layer 1: System prompt rules (15 editorial rules baked into every generation)**

The system prompt contains explicit, negation-based rules. Not "write well" — that's useless. Instead:

* Never name an emotion after showing it physically (the show-then-tell-then-tell problem)
* No character speaks for more than 3 consecutive sentences without interruption
* Maximum one significant piece of new information per response
* Every new location gets at least two senses described, not just visual
* Each NPC has a NEVER SAYS list — phrases that character would never use, which constrains the voice more effectively than describing what they would say

Negative constraints outperform positive instructions by a wide margin in my testing. The model already knows how to write well. It doesn't know your specific failure modes.

**Layer 2: Client-side regex filter (275+ patterns, zero API cost, zero latency)**

This runs on every AI response after generation but before display. It's deterministic — no API call, no latency, no cost. The filter:

* Caps em dashes at 2 per response, converts excess to commas
* Converts semicolons to periods
* Detects show-then-tell patterns (physical cue followed by emotion naming) and strips the emotion naming
* Caps "something cold settled/crawled/spread" at 1 per response
* Caps body-emotion markers ("stomach dropped", "chest tightened") at 2 per response
* Caps facial choreography ("expression darkened", "gaze softened") at 2 per response
* Auto-replaces \~15 confirmed AI clichés with randomised alternatives (so the fix doesn't become its own detectable pattern)
* Detects AI-default vocabulary and flags it
* Strips perception filters after the first instance ("she noticed", "he observed" — just describe the thing directly)

The randomised replacement is important. If you replace "blood turned to ice" with "cold moved through her" every time, you've just created a new fingerprint. Instead, we pick from 3-4 alternatives randomly.

**Layer 3: Per-character Voice DNA**

This is the hardest part. Getting one consistent AI voice is easy. Getting 4-5 distinct NPC voices in the same generation is genuinely difficult — the model wants to converge on a single register.

Each NPC gets a voice specification injected into the system prompt:

* **Register** (formal-clinical, casual-sardonic, warm-anxious, polished-corporate)
* **Sentence length range** (short and clipped vs. long and parenthetical)
* **Rhythm** (military cadence vs. academic consideration vs. nervous rushing)
* **Verbal tics** (specific physical behaviours — "dries the same glass repeatedly when thinking", "flips a coin when bored")
* **Metaphor domain** (what domain their comparisons draw from — a military character says "perimeter", "compromised", "secured"; a medical character says "metastasised", "excise the problem")
* **NEVER SAYS list** (things this specific character would never say)

The metaphor domain and NEVER SAYS list are the highest-impact fields. They create the most distinctiveness per token spent.

**Layer 4: Continuity Ledger — structured state tracking**

Every interactive fiction engine hits the context window problem. After 20-30 exchanges, the model starts forgetting established facts. Our solution is a structured JSON ledger that tracks:

* Current scene (location, time, weather, ambient details)
* Which NPCs are present and their emotional states
* What the player knows and doesn't know
* What each NPC knows (and what they're withholding)
* A queue of pending story beats with priority levels (critical/important/optional)
* Trust scores per NPC that shift based on player actions
* A consequence queue (delayed effects of past decisions)
* Pacing metrics (exchanges since last significant event)

After each exchange, a lightweight API call analyses what changed and updates the ledger. The ledger is then injected into the next prompt as structured constraints, not prose summary. This means the 50th exchange has the same factual accuracy as the 5th.

**Layer 5: Adaptive Narrative Engine — 11 GM principles**

This is where it goes from "chatbot with rules" to something that feels like a game. We codified 11 principles from tabletop RPG game master best practices:

The ones that had the biggest impact on player experience:

* **Never Block the Player** — if the player attempts an action, it happens. Introduce consequences and complications, but never "you can't do that." The narrative bends around the player's choices.
* **Relocatable Story Beats** — beats aren't tied to locations. If the player skips the cave where the revelation was planned, the revelation moves to wherever they go next. The seams must be invisible.
* **NPC Initiative** — NPCs aren't furniture. If the player hasn't interacted with an NPC for several exchanges, that NPC acts on their own agenda. The world doesn't wait for the player to drive everything.
* **Telegraph Before Escalate** — before something bad happens, provide warning signs. Players should see danger coming and choose whether to engage.
* **Consequences, Not Punishment** — every choice has ripple effects, but they're natural, not punitive. Clever solutions are rewarded. Reckless choices create complications but never dead ends.

The pacing system is particularly interesting from a game design perspective. It tracks exchanges since the last significant event. If the story stalls (6+ exchanges of nothing happening), the system prompt tells the model to deploy a pending beat or have an NPC take initiative. If events are stacking too fast, it inserts a breathing moment. This prevents both the "nothing is happening" stall and the "too much is happening" overwhelm.

**Layer 6: Slash commands for player agency**

Players can steer the narrative with commands: /darker, /lighter, /complication, /timeskip, /introduce (new character), /npc (force NPC initiative), /scene (change location), /flashback. These inject directives into the system prompt for the next generation. It gives the player meta-control over pacing and tone without breaking the fourth wall.

**What I learned:**

1. **Prompt engineering has a ceiling. Post-processing closes the gap.** No system prompt, no matter how detailed, produces 100% compliance. The client-side filter catches the last 5-10%.
2. **Negative constraints > positive instructions.** "Never use em dashes more than twice" works. "Write with varied punctuation" doesn't.
3. **The model's biggest weakness in interactive fiction is convergence.** It wants every scene to become a confrontation. Every NPC to give information freely. Every paragraph to end with an em dash. The entire architecture is essentially an anti-convergence system.
4. **Structured state beats prose summary.** A JSON ledger injected as constraints is more reliable than "here's what happened so far" as a paragraph.
5. **Haiku-class models + heavy prompt engineering + client-side filtering = Sonnet-class output quality at 1/10th the cost.** We run Haiku for all RP exchanges. The editorial system does the quality work. This makes the economics viable at scale.

**The game is live at** [**ghostproof.uk/rp**](https://ghostproof.uk/rp) **— free to play, 20 exchanges/day, no account needed.**

There are 9 scenarios across different genres (medical thriller, fantasy, cosmic horror, cyberpunk, western, gothic romance, supernatural anime, contemporary mystery, sci-fi). 19 playable species. 8 character classes. 80+ NPCs with unique voice profiles.

When you first arrive, you meet the Doorkeeper — a sardonic gatekeeper NPC. He's a good 2-minute test of the voice system and editorial quality.

I'd love feedback from game devs on the narrative systems specifically — does the pacing feel managed without feeling railroaded? Do the NPCs feel distinct from each other? Are there AI patterns the filter is still missing?

Happy to go deeper on any part of the architecture.

comments.author: wadrasil
comments.body: I remember reading the elements of style in English composition and it seems like you wrote more instructions for ai than generally needed for people.

replies.author: Jaycool2k
replies.body:
That's actually the exact insight that drives the whole system. Strunk & White works for humans because humans have taste, they can read "omit needless words" and *feel* what that means. They have a lifetime of reading to pattern-match against.

LLMs don't have taste. They have probability distributions. So "write clearly" means nothing, but "never follow a physical reaction with an emotion label" produces an immediate, measurable change in output quality. Every rule in the system is essentially a Strunk & White principle translated into the kind of explicit, mechanical instruction that a statistical model can actually comply with.

The irony is that the *output* reads more human precisely because the instructions are less human. You have to be robotic about the rules to get prose that isn't.

replies.author: Jaycool2k
replies.body:
You caught em dashes in a post about catching em dashes. That's exactly the kind of pattern recognition the system is built for — so genuinely, well spotted.

But the claim isn't that I wrote this post with the engine. The claim is that when an LLM generates fiction — 200 exchanges deep into a medical thriller where a character is hiding a USB drive — it defaults to em dashes every third sentence, names emotions after showing them physically, and makes every NPC sound like the same polite narrator wearing different hats. That's what the filter catches.

The difference between a human using em dashes as a stylistic habit and an LLM using them as a statistical default is frequency and distribution. I used them maybe 8 times in 1,500 words of technical writing. An unfiltered LLM will produce 5-6 per 300-word fiction response. The filter caps it at 2. That's the gap.

Easiest way to test whether I'm full of it: ghostproof.uk/rp. Talk to the Doorkeeper. Two minutes, free, no account. If it reads like ChatGPT in a costume, I deserve every word of this comment. If it doesn't — then the architecture works regardless of how many em dashes I used to describe it. 

Here's part of Chapter 1 from a thriller that went through the engine. The editorial filter caught 14 patterns in the raw generation. This is what came out the other side. Count the em dashes if you like — I'll wait.

CHAPTER 1

The first sensation that clawed its way through the fog was cold. Not the gentle bite of winter air, but something deeper, more invasive, seeping through fabric and flesh to settle in my bones like a living thing. I opened my eyes to a ceiling of rough-hewn timber, dark beams stretching across whitewashed planks that seemed to swim in and out of focus. The light filtering through nearby windows held that peculiar quality of snow-reflected illumination, bright yet somehow muted, as if the world beyond had been wrapped in gauze.

I tried to piece together where I was, how I'd come to be lying on what felt like polished hardwood beneath me, but my thoughts moved like treacle, thick and uncooperative. The back of my skull throbbed with each heartbeat, a percussion that seemed to echo through the floorboards and up into my body. When I attempted to sit up, the room tilted violently to the left. I gripped the floor with both hands until the sensation passed.

That's when I noticed my clothing.

I wore surgical scrubs, the pale green kind favoured in operating theatres, but they hung wrong on my frame. Too loose through the shoulders, too short in the arms. The fabric felt expensive. Far nicer than anything I'd worn in my years as a paramedic. Dark patches covered the front of the shirt. Some dried to a rusty brown, others still damp enough to smell metallic when I brought the material closer to my nose.

Blood. Unmistakably blood.

My hands shook as I examined the stains more closely. They weren't the chaotic splashes you'd expect from trauma work. I'd seen plenty of those over the years. These were different. Methodical. As if someone had been working carefully and something had gone wrong.

I pushed myself to my feet. The world tilted again before settling into an uneasy equilibrium.

A stone fireplace dominated one wall, cold ash scattered across the hearth like grey snow that had forgotten how to fall. The ash looked recent. Someone had burned papers here, and not long ago. Fragments of what might have been medical forms curled among the debris, their edges blackened but still legible enough to make out partial words: patient, protocol, threshold. Heavy furniture upholstered in deep burgundy occupied the space with the solid presence of things built to last, but everything felt staged, like a movie set dressed to look lived-in rather than actually inhabited.

None of it felt familiar. The complete absence of recognition hit me like a closed fist.

I reached into the pockets of the scrubs, hoping for some clue. My fingers found a leather wallet, expensive and well-worn. I pulled it out with trembling hands and flipped it open.

The photograph on the driving licence showed a face I didn't recognise. A man perhaps ten years older than my thirty-two, with salt-and-pepper hair and intelligent eyes behind wire-rimmed spectacles. The name made me stagger backward until my legs hit the edge of a sofa.

Dr. Vincent Halloway.

Why was I carrying another man's identity? And why couldn't I remember anything beyond waking up on this floor?

I tried to grasp at memories, but they slipped away like water through my fingers. The last clear recollection was Tuesday or Wednesday. I'd been working a shift with David, my partner. We'd responded to a call about chest pains in Whitechapel, an elderly woman having an anxiety attack rather than a heart episode. After that, nothing. A void where days should have been.

That was all I could remember of whatever had happened next.

I sat back on the sofa, staring at Halloway's credentials. In my line of work, you learned to trust your memory, to catalogue details that might save lives. The absence of it felt like losing a limb. How could you fight against not knowing? My hands were shaking worse now because I understood this wasn't just confusion. It was something deliberate. Someone had taken my memory, my time, my identity. Someone had dressed me in surgical scrubs and left me here with a dead man's wallet.

But I was still hungry. Christ, when had I last eaten? The thought arrived unbidden and absurd. Here I was, trapped in some nightmare scenario, and my stomach was registering that I hadn't eaten in days. The mundane concern felt almost obscene, yet it anchored me.

I was still Cole Brennan. Still someone with a body that needed feeding.

If I was going to survive this, I needed to think like a paramedic. Assess, investigate, gather intelligence.

I needed to search this place systematically. The main room yielded few answers. Good quality linens, expensive crockery, bottles of wine that probably cost more than I made in a week. But there were oddities. A locked cabinet that rattled when I shook it. A desk drawer holding prescription pads, all bearing the name Dr. Vincent Halloway.

The kitchen adjoined the main room through an archway. Here the strangeness deepened. On the worktop, arranged with surgical precision, sat equipment I recognised from my paramedic training. IV bags, syringes, vials of medications I couldn't identify without closer examination. Someone had been preparing for medical procedures, serious ones by the look of it. The professional arrangement suggested whoever had been working here knew exactly what they were doing.

comments.author: Beautiful-Arugula-44
comments.body:
So.. from my side:

1) It sounds like AI quite a lot. There is vast use of typical sentence structures like  
"not A... but B..."  
"A <does X> the way B <does Z>  
These are just veery AI--typical terms to phrase analogies.  
I'm not saying that it sounds bad.. but it does not sound human-esque at all.

2) I like it a lot!! The way the story integrates my words and my actions feels very convincing. Whatever I say, it feels like a natural part of the story as it should have been carried out anyway. This feels like magic. It's playful and immersive. I had a lot of fun!!

3) The NPCs don't feel very distinct to each other. The way they talk, their vocabulary, their attitude.. it does not feel unique. I could imagine single NPCs to have more different traits, resulting in more different ways to speak and interact.

4) I don't feel attached to the character I created, at all. All these attributes and information. It evens feels more like a Tabulara Rasa: Do anything you want. The character and its stats seem to be of very limited importance. Maybe you would want to show and share all these situations when a player  roke (just like it habbens

replies.author: Jaycool2k
replies.body:
Firstly thank you so much for taking the time to test and play around with it. As you can see it's still in early build mode but feedback like this is so very important. 

1) You're identifying something the current filter doesn't catch, the structural patterns vs vocabulary patterns. The filter handles word-level tells (em dashes, perception filters, show-then-tell) but you're right that sentence-level constructions like "not A... but B..." and "A does X the way B does Z" are equally detectable as AI-default. They're the grammatical equivalent of an em dash, but statistically overrepresented. That's going on the development list.

2) 'This feels like magic' is just what I like to hear. I'm so glad you enjoyed the quick click around to see what is being built on. Did you enjoy the doorkeeper? I kept having fun conversations with him seeing if I can wind him up. I am just really happy it was time well spent and you enjoyed it.

3) Each NPC has a voice specification (register, sentence length, metaphor domain, verbal tics, a "never says" list) but you're right that the distinctiveness isn't landing consistently. The model wants to converge on a single voice. & that's the hardest problem in multi-character AI fiction. I'm going to look at the structure and see what I can do. Which scenario did you play?

4) This is a new addition to the build which I am working on, so I understand the lack of attachment to the character. The visible stat checks that show inline when a stat matters. Instead of the stats being invisible prompt guidance, you'll soon see something like "\[CHECK: Eloquence | 4 | 3 | success\]" rendered as a badge when the narrative hinges on one of your stats. It makes the RPG layer feel mechanical instead of decorative. The character attachment problem is harder (not going to lie).  I think the fix will show moments where your specific character build changed the outcome. "You succeeded here because your Insight is 4. A character with Insight 2 would have missed this." Making the build feel consequential. That's next on the list.

Thank you again for the feedback! It's really appreciated!

replies.author: Beautiful-Arugula-44
replies.body:
You're very welcome. I had a lot of fun so far!

Well done!

You don't seem to get much attention for some of the posts.

I guess many redditors assume some kind of "low effort project". But, to me, Ghostproof RP seems to be a quite solid foundation and a promising setup. Also, it's quite promising how much you are seeking feedback, instead of just spreading the word. Keep up the good work! :)

Re: 4: hahah, oops, NOW i realize that i forgot to finish the last sentences. i actually fell asleep while typing, but then sent the comment ;D - well, i originally wanted to suggest exactly what you now teased in your answer: to have way more stat checks, similar to Disco Elysium (DE). maybe not only for the "decisive" parts, but also for the "descriptive" parts. i personally liked that the most with DE: to see how my stats / my inner world alters how i PERCEIVE the world (and thereby how i can interact with it). one side idea: maybe the choice between "dark" or "friendly" narration style also could be a character trait (stat). i would be 100% sold if an AI narrative game let's me chose and develop stats like Inland Empire, Drama, Conceptualization etc. - just like in DE. LLMs are perfectly tailored for this. some more stats (similar to DE-attributes) that may be more interesting than classic attributes like "Strength" etc. with regards to LLM-driven narration emergence  that come to my mind: Melancholia, Lunacy, Quaintness, Brilliance, Freigeist, Probity, Brilliance, Neuroticism, Depth, Vigilance,.. just my idea dump, just in case sth resonates with you and inspires you : )

Re: 3: I played (or, better: still am playing) the "Paper Gods" scenario.

replies.author: Jaycool2k
replies.body:
The Disco Elysium comparison is exactly where my head has been going. The stats shouldn't just gate success / failure, they should alter how the narrator describes the world to you. A character with high Insight doesn't just succeed at noticing things. They perceive the world differently. The prose itself changes.

Your stat suggestions are going straight in, would you be happy to be credited as the person who guided me? Melancholia, Lunacy, Quaintness, Brilliance, Freigeist, Probity, Neuroticism, Depth & Vigilance, those feel like they belong in a system where the stats are the narrator's voice, not just numbers the narrator checks against.

Paper Gods is a great scenario for this kind of perception-driven play. Oboro's dialogue changes depending on whether you're observant or trusting. The shrine itself responds differently to different kinds of attention. I'm really glad you're playing that one, and it's the newest and one I'm most interested in hearing feedback on.

The DE-style perception stats are going on the development roadmap. The build already supports it, the stat values are injected into every system prompt, so making the narrator write differently based on stat levels is a prompt engineering problem, not an infrastructure problem. The hard part is making it feel as seamless as DE did, where you genuinely couldn't tell where the stat ended and the writing began.

Thank you for falling asleep mid-feedback and still sending it! That might be the most honest review I've ever received. Keep playing Paper Gods and let me know how Oboro treats you, as she's watching. 👀

replies.author: Beautiful-Arugula-44
replies.body:
Sounds great! :) Yes, I will continue playing soon, and be glad to drop some further feedback on "Paper Gods"!

Regarding the attributes, I will just quickly share my list with you. Actually, I was thinking of a similar game concept to yours. That's where I pull these from. Yet, I am obviously not realising it. So, if some of these ideas live on in your project, I'm just happy :-)

Feel free to use them as you wish. No credit needed.

|Attribute|Familiar Concepts|Description|
|:-|:-|:-|
|**Vigilance**|Alertness, Awareness, Perception, Situational Awareness, Attunement|You register the slightest shift in the world: a flicker in the corner of your eye, a tone half a note off. The outside speaks constantly - this is your ability to listen before it screams.|
|**Divergence**|Creativity, Lateral Thinking, Improvisation, Possibility Space, Co-Creation|You see the world in superposition. Every situation fractures into alternatives, and you instinctively weave new paths and interconnections - sometimes together with others, sometimes against them.|
|**Depth**|Intensity, Gravity, Emotional Weight, Existential Awareness, Immersion|Experiences don’t pass through you - they sink in with urgent weight. You don't feel the surface beneath your feet. You feel the roots that entangle the layers.|
|**Lunacy**|Madness, Absurdity, Surrealism, Delusion, Cosmic Irony|You see what does not make sense. Not in a psychotic way. You just reveal and embrace alternative meanings. Where others see routine or chaos, you get in touch with the constructivist machinery of existence itself.|
|**Quaintness**|Eccentricity, Oddness, Idiosyncrasy, Unconventionality, Peculiarity|You don't put things in perspective; you put them off-axis. To you, differences are intricate, complex, beautiful. You do not align. You give birth to dancing stars.|
|**Neuroticism**|Anxiety, Rumination, Insecurity, Sensitivity, Inner Turmoil|Your mind circles its own shadows. Thoughts spiral, doubts multiply, and emotions linger longer than they should. It is this friction, that sharpens your perception in uncomfortable but powerful ways.|
|**Friskiness**|Playfulness, Whimsy, Childlike Wonder, Mischief, Lightness|Even in darkness, you find something to poke, to laugh at, to play with. A stubborn spark insists that existence is, at least partly, a game. And you are the kind of people, who dare to play with the rules.|
|**Brilliance**|Pattern Recognition, Insight, Overthinking, Hyper-Analysis, Apophenia|Connections bloom everywhere. You assemble meaning at high speed - sometimes illuminating hidden truths, sometimes inventing patterns that were never there.|
|**Freigeist**|Autonomy, Independence, Nonconformity, Detachment, Self-Direction|No anchor holds you for long. You move by your own compass, resisting structures that try to define or contain you. Freedom is both your strength and your isolation.|
|**Probity**|Integrity, Justice, Moral Compass, Honesty, Conscience|A quiet but persistent voice measures right from wrong. You feel the weight of fairness, and even when it costs you, you hesitate to betray it.|

|**Freigeist**|Autonomy, Independence, Nonconformity, Detachment, Self-Direction|No anchor holds you for long. You move by your own compass, resisting structures that try to define or contain you. Freedom is both your strength and your isolation.|
